summary: Describes how to use HTTP over TLS as a dereference protocol that resolves a reference to a PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format Location Object). The Location Recipient is assumed to hold a URI that works with the HELD protocol. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Instead of telling everyone where you are, you hand out a link. Whoever has the link can securely ask a server where you are right now.

questions: how to dereference a location uri with held
how to dereference a location uri
does held dereference support get requests
subtitle: How a holder of a location URI uses HTTP over TLS and a slice of HELD to fetch the location behind it.

tldr.problem: Sometimes a device passes around a link to its location instead of the location itself. The party holding that link needs a standard way to turn it into an actual location.
tldr.mechanism: The holder sends a restricted HELD locationRequest over HTTPS to the location URI, or simply an HTTP GET, and the Location Server answers with a PIDF-LO location document. Access is controlled by keeping the URI secret.
tldr.outcome: It defines a small, privacy-minded profile of HELD for dereferencing. It specifies no way to authenticate recipients, so it relies on possession of the URI as the authorization.

today: RFC 6753 is a Proposed Standard and the data shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves recipient authentication to future specifications.

sections.title: Dereferencing a Location URI
sections.content:
A location URI identifies a resource that holds the location of an entity. RFC 6753 says how the holder of an http: or https: location URI uses it to get that location, using either a subset of the HELD protocol or a plain HTTP GET request.

Such a URI can be obtained through a location configuration protocol, for example HELD itself (RFC 5985) or a DHCP location URI option. What comes back is a PIDF-LO document (RFC 4119), the standard presence-based format for a location object.

Supporting HTTP GET is mandatory so that the URI still works for a client that does not know it is a location URI. Clients that do know can use HELD parameters to say what kind of location they want, within limits.
sections.eli5: Imagine a note that says 'ask this mailbox where I am'. This document explains how to ask the mailbox, and what kind of answer you get back.

sections.title: The HELD Usage Profile
sections.content:
Using HELD to dereference is largely the same as using it for configuration, with restrictions. The only request allowed is locationRequest. The Location Server (LS) must not accept request parameters other than responseTime and locationType (including its exact attribute).

The LS must ignore parameters it does not understand unless it knows them to be invalid, in which case it may return a HELD error. Parameters from RFC 6155 are always invalid here. Importantly, the LS must not create location URIs or return a locationUriSet in answer to a dereference request.

The connection follows RFC 2818. The URI scheme decides whether TLS is used. Servers must be configured to issue only HTTPS URIs and answer only HTTPS requests, unless confidentiality and integrity come from something else, such as a trusted network or an IPsec channel. With TLS, the TLS_NULL_WITH_NULL_NULL ciphersuite must not be used and the LS must be authenticated.

A plain http: URI usually gives too little security: the Rule Maker loses control over who receives the location, and the recipient cannot trust the answer.
sections.eli5: The rules say you can only ask a few simple questions, and the server cannot hand out new links. The conversation should be in a locked, private tunnel.

sections.title: HTTP GET Behavior
sections.content:
Ordinary HTTP clients send GET, whereas HELD normally uses POST. Instead of replying with 405 (Method Not Allowed), a LIS must return a HELD location response to a GET.

A GET is treated as if a locationRequest with a locationType of geodetic civic and exact="false" had been POSTed. GET requests must be safe and idempotent: repeating one may return a different location, but only because the Target moved, not because of any side effect. Since no location URI can be created by a request to a location URI, this holds.

A recipient may infer that a URI supports HELD if the response has the content type application/held+xml. Servers may support content negotiation: sending an Accept header that includes application/pidf+xml returns the presence document directly in the body, without the locationResponse wrapper.
sections.eli5: If you just open the link in a normal way, the server still gives you the answer instead of complaining that you asked the wrong way.

sections.title: Authorization Models
sections.content:
The document discusses two extreme models and does not mandate one. In both, the Target gets a location URI from the LIS, conveys it to a Location Recipient (for example over SIP, RFC 6442), and the recipient dereferences it. The LS then decides whether to answer.

Authorization by possession treats knowledge of the URI as the credential. The URI should be hard to guess, disclosed to few parties and protected from eavesdroppers. Authorization is hard to revoke once granted, so expiry of the URI is a useful limit.

Authorization via access control uses an explicit policy set by the Rule Maker, so the URI can be given to many recipients. Policy formats such as Common Policy (RFC 4745) can express this.

This RFC defines no authentication mechanism for recipients, so access control by identity is not an option. It assumes authorization by possession. A Rule Maker can still give each recipient a different URI with a different policy, which acts as a stand-in for identity-based rules. A server may support an authentication mechanism, and future specifications may define one.
sections.eli5: One way is a secret treehouse password: anyone who knows it gets in. The other is a guest list at the door. Here there is no way to check names, so the password way is used.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The overall flow is: the device asks the LIS for a location URI, hands the URI to the recipient, and the recipient asks the LIS for the location. The RFC walks through this with the example URI https://ls.example.com:49152/uri/w3g61nf5n66p0.

The simplest dereference is a POST of an empty locationRequest to that path. The example response lists both civic and geodetic information for the Target in a PIDF-LO. Unless policy says otherwise, the recipient gets the same information the device would have received.

The same URI can be fetched with a GET, which the LS treats as the request in Figure 1. A GET with Accept: application/pidf+xml,application/held+xml;q=0.5 returns the bare PIDF-LO as application/pidf+xml.
sections.eli5: You can ask by filling in a form (POST) or just by knocking (GET). Either way you get a note saying where the person is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Privacy of location information is the main concern, and two measures protect it: TLS and authorization policies. TLS must be used unless confidentiality and integrity are provided another way. Recipients must authenticate the host using the domain name in the location URI, as in Section 3.1 of RFC 2818; local policy decides what happens if that fails or cannot be tried.

Under authorization by possession, the URI is a secret, so it too needs TLS in transit, and it must only be disclosed to authorized recipients. Holding the URI carries the same privacy implications as holding the PIDF-LO itself.

The LS must not reveal anything about the Target except location unless Rule Maker policy allows it. In particular it must use only an unlinked pseudonym in the entity attribute of the PIDF-LO unless policy permits identity disclosure. The appendices map the design against GEOPRIV and location-by-reference requirements; they note it is not compliant with the single-message-transfer goal, and that it supports unlimited repeat resolution until the URI expires.
sections.eli5: The main rule is: keep the secret link secret, use a locked tunnel, and never put the person's name on the answer.
